title: The One Who's Not Busy, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of approaching practice with openness, awareness, and gratitude, rather than trying to control or avoid distractions. This involves recognizing the impermanence of thoughts and emotions, allowing them to arise and pass without judgment, and cultivating a sense of "not busy" or effortless awareness. By letting go of our preconceptions and habitual perceptions, we can begin to see reality with fresh eyes, leading to liberation from suffering and a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world around us.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
Welcome.
Welcome, our guests.
Do you like what we've done with the place?

Several of you have mentioned that you found the practice of breath counting helpful: counting the exhalations gently, one, two, three, maybe to ten, trying to remember it's not a competition with yourself.
But the tricky thing is that it's hard to tell whether a practice is helpful, isn't it?
Sometimes in our subjective experience we have a result we like.
You feel like you can concentrate better, you're not so anxious, something pleasant.
Other times we have a subjective experience in practice that we don't like.
One practice or the other feels boring, or mechanical, or frustrating, or dubious in some way.
Everyone's a critic.
But the tricky thing is that the practice you don't like, especially in the short term, may turn out to be the most helpful.
So how do we know how to practice?
It's pretty clear by now that this whole thing is not just about indulging our preferences and trying to get things the way we like them, right?
Because that's why we're here practicing in the first place.
We tried living that way, I think.
Have you tried that way?
Probably.
And it doesn't always work out somehow.
Weird, despite what it says and all the information we're mostly exposed to.
So how do we know what helps?
Is there a feeling to it, maybe, that's deeper than just preferences?
A sense of connection, or we were talking yesterday about a sense of groundedness, as a complement to our smart, cognitive, egocentric self that we also need and treasure.
In any case, why bother with any kind of technique?
Isn't this Zen thing all about just sitting anyway?
Why would we need something extra, like counting your breath?
Why not just sit?
Well, I think that's fine.
That's good, if in fact we're really just sitting.

Finding some way of deeply just being, just letting everything drop away, opening to the wide possibilities that emerge moment by moment without too much stickiness or aversion, just being so present.
That's wonderful, and maybe in some way that's our deep practice.
But sometimes "I just want to sit," if we're honest, means I just want to space out.
I just want to check out.
It's hard to know.
Maybe sometimes it's skillful to check out for a while, right?
Everybody needs a break.
That's what's funny about the whole meditation business anyway.
The teachers and your peers, the scientists, if they're trying to study meditation: nobody has any idea what's going on in your head anyway, much less you.
So it turns out that most of the instruction in Zen is quite individual.
Sometimes it can help to just bring it up with the teacher and see what emerges in the conversation.
Sometimes, if I'm in the teacher's seat, I have some sense of clarity, but it's not exactly me that sees that.
There's something in that openness and that vulnerability in sharing our experience.
Something arises sometimes in the conversation, and sometimes there's a sense that pops out of my mouth, if I'm in that role: "That sounds really pleasant, great, continue."
Or, "Oh, that sounds really unpleasant, please continue anyway."
Or, "That sounds really unpleasant, don't do that anymore.
That's not helping."
I don't know.
Do I know?
Do you know?
But somehow in a way we can know sometimes.

Sometimes that works really beautifully and gives a fresh perspective that [unclear: "tries you might"] to figure it all out on your own, and we're so conditioned to figuring everything out on our own.
You're just spinning your wheels.
But then other times in the interview room I really have no clue.
If I'm feeling grounded and clear, maybe I'll actually say that: "Hmm, I don't know, sorry, no idea."
Other times I just feel frustrated and vulnerable and a little bit inadequate.
I really want to be helpful with people, and I know you do too.
So in the Dokusan room I especially want to be helpful, but it's not always possible.
How could it be?
For two complex human beings to deeply meet in a couple of minutes and feel our way towards more clarity, this is a tall order, and it's amazing that it works as often as it does.
Don't you think?
And it's very vulnerable for both people.
It's very vulnerable for all of us doing this kind of practice, no matter what we're doing: sitting in our seat, in the kitchen, walking down the garden or the jungle path there, the forest path.
It's very vulnerable.
I was especially appreciating the vulnerability of doing new kinds of roles and positions and jobs, which is a big part of what we do.
To have our days in silence, we constellate a complex little society with lots of different roles and jobs so that it all runs smoothly and we can eat and walk and sleep and sit and all this.
I always appreciate this, but in this small, intimate sesshin that we're having this time, I especially appreciate that so many of us are doing something that's new to them.
And that's pretty vulnerable.
And some of us are doing a role that it appears we have done before, and yet doing it with such freshness, don't you think?
Such energy and verve, ringing those bells or whatever it is.
But it's a situation in which we're vulnerable and we're exposed.
And somehow we often feel very exposed and vulnerable when we have to talk to each other, right?
I suspect we happen to be a selection of the broader population that's not that comfortable at parties, for instance.
That might be true.
And so you would think, oh, thank goodness, no talking.
But then it turns out that we're even more vulnerable than if we're yammering around.
Nowhere to hide.
There's a commentary line in one of the other Zen stories that's been in my mind a lot lately.
The commentary line is "completely exposed, completely exposed."
And I realized yesterday, at one point when I was walking back to my little trailer, that I myself am doing a new role in this sesshin.
This is the first multi-day sesshin I've ever led without another Dharma teacher.
Usually I'd be co-teaching with Echo Jeff Kelly from Seattle, Soto Zen, or my teacher Norman Fischer, or somebody.
Of course, I've led all kinds of things by myself.
But in our tradition, the multi-day sesshin, especially the residential sesshin where we're living here, is like the big kahuna, the deepest ritual.
And it is a ritual; this whole thing is a ritual.
So it's seen as a very big deal to be the teacher leading it.
I didn't think of that until I got here.
I'm like, oh, my goodness, how about that?
Which I think is great.
I think with all of our steps forward in life and in practice, it's best if it's that way.
You just take the next step and you're just going along, and suddenly you realize, oh, my goodness, I'm married now.
Wow.
I'm doing this job.
Wow.
I appear to have published an article or a book.
How did that happen?
Wow.
My name's on the cover.
But then we also recognize, when we do some big new thing, that we're not really doing it ourselves.
I'm not actually leading this alone.

I feel, know, and can see, looking around, that I'm really surrounded and supported, just part of a matrix and a web full of deeply experienced, thoughtful people, colleagues, some of whom I've had the pleasure to practice with for decades.
Pleasure and occasional challenge, I guess, is the honest answer.
And there's so much leadership here.
I love that we try in our little way, on the one hand, to honor the structures, and yes, they are hierarchical.
I don't know if that's inherently a bad word or not.
So honor these structures and leadership systems and roles and so on, and make the best use of them we can.
I think it's pretty efficient, for one thing.
It would have been a bummer if all 18 of us had to have three meetings before we could come here.
To honor that, but then we also try to do everything we do pretty cooperatively, to do it together.
So that spirit is here, I think.
Don't you think?
We had a major kitchen help person have to withdraw at the last minute, and then I turn around and there's all these people in the kitchen anyway.
So cooperative.
Are you getting enough help, Bob?
Okay.
And yet it is true that this role of the teacher is an important role.
There's also just one role, one role of many.

Our emptiness teachings remind us of the really important and true fact that being the teacher is not in any qualitative way different from being the cook or the bell ringer or the cabin trim painter.
All these roles have an essence of essentialness.
It's the same.
And there's also something important to this role, so I'll just do my best.
Not that I feel like I'm a brilliant Zen master, but I seem to have had the karma to wear the right gear and sit in the right spot.
So I'll sit there.
In case I forget to say this later, if any of my words or deeds confuse you or are harmful or unhelpful, I apologize for that.
And I always invite you to let me know.
I'll try to learn.
And I'll try also, as best I can, to recognize if it's not actually me, but something else anyway.
It's hard to discern, though, isn't it?
So anyway, it's another long-winded way of saying thank you for being here.
Gratitude in the end is kind of like our main practice.
Speaking of practice, you could just stick to breath counting if you've taken it up.
And if you haven't yet, please do.
It's a good practice to stick with for a whole sesshin for sure, or for some months or years.
Or, I can't resist making another suggestion: you could try a companion practice to breath counting, what I might provisionally call open awareness of breathing.

When you first sit down, tune in strongly, as you have been, to breath and body, aligning yourself and really opening up the system if it's shut down, and really feeling where you are, breathing, body, on this spot of the planet.
But then allow the breath awareness that you have connected to to be lighter and lighter.
Hold it so gently.
Just let the body breathe.
It doesn't need you to tell it what to do.
There's just breathing happening, and you have the great good fortune to be present.
In this lighter, more open awareness of breathing, one thing that's a little different is how you relate to so-called distractions.
Oftentimes in breath counting, you're on two and you start thinking about something and you say, no, no, no.
Back to breath counting.
One.
There's a sense of noticing and moving away, which is a good thing to do.
But it's also great, when the mind is somewhere other than resting lightly on the breathing, not to be the least bit aversive to this other state.
Instead of seeing something as a distraction, which is a judgment, right, just see that there's another phenomenon arising in the mind.
Here it is.
Let it be a little more like weather.
Clouds drifting through the mind, occasionally rain squalls or a quick thunderstorm.
Just let other mind states and thoughts and drifty dreamies and space-outs, or whatever it is that you call them, pass through the mind.
And there's the feeling of just gently, organically and naturally settling back, like it just happens without thinking about it.
Settling back on the breath awareness of light.
So not so much this strong moving away from distractions and back to the breath, but more like allowing.
Being with, opening to.
Naturally, organically, you find yourself there.
You don't even need to have the thought, oh, I'm breathing.
Nah, that's extra.
That's like a little bird flying by or something.
I'm breathing.
Oh, okay.
Ah.
Good job.
Bad job.
But it's nice to be deliberate in zazen.
Are you practicing, in each period of meditation: am I practicing breath counting this time?
Sticking with that.
Maybe this lighter, open awareness of breathing.
It's nice to make a choice and stick with it.
And just to add another little bit of confusion, you could also do both together.
First ten minutes, breath counting, settling the space.
And then just transition lightly: breath counting, quiet, quiet, gentle breath counting.
Oh, there's no more counting needed.
Just breathing.
Watching what happens.
Oh, where was I?
Back to breath counting.
So you can play a little bit, and we can talk about it if you like.
But it's good to be deliberate.
We're not just sitting around, in other words.
In all these practices, let's invite forward the spirit of Yunyan's "You should know there's one who's not busy."
Let's just tell that story again.
It's so worthy of repeat.
These two monks were together.
One named Yunyan was sweeping.
His brother monk, Dao, comes up and says, "Mmm, too busy."
Yunyan looks up and says, "You should know there's one who's not busy."
Dao says, "If so, then there's a second moon."
The first one holds up his broom and says, "Oh, which moon is this?"
I always imagine he flips the broom over.
It doesn't say that.
Just the hand wouldn't look right.
So it's probably, whoo, "Which moon is this?"
So let's remember to apply the spirit of not busy in our zazen practice too.
Noticing when we constrict into a busy, tense, effortful, frustrating, whatever state.
But then, when that is present, can we treat it a little bit like the second way of practicing that I just mentioned?
Not as a problem or a failure.
It's just more weather in the mind.
Oh, yeah.
Yep.
One.
Yep.
Or you could even ask yourself, imagining this broom, "Which moon is this?
Which moon is this?
Who's the one who's not busy here?"
The second moon is a metaphor from a Chinese sutra, and I want to make good on my promise and tell you what that's about.
So I'm going to indulge in a little bit of a long digression, which hopefully will be interesting.
And if you sleep through this next part, it's on the recording.
It's a reference from a Chinese sutra called the Shurangama Sutra, which is a longish Mahayana sutra.
Here it is, translated in English. [unclear: "Hefty tone"].
A little bit of commentary in it, but it's most of the sutra.
This whole sutra is an exploration of the nature of reality that mostly happens in a long, long dialogue between Buddha and Ananda.
Ananda, as you may know, was Buddha's cousin and his primary attendant, his Jisha, you would say.
Ananda has long been my favorite of the early disciples of the Buddha.
He was brilliant and devoted, a really smart guy with an incredible memory.
In the early Buddhist days they didn't write down the teachings.
I think they had some simple writing systems for merchants and numbers and stuff.
Although as I say that, I know there are some ancient Indian texts that are really, really old.
In any case, the Buddhist teachings were not written down.
So the conceit is that Ananda memorized all of it, everything the Buddha ever said, and could repeat it.
Lots of the other monks memorized it too.
You want to do those a couple maybe?
Okay.
Alright.
It's going to be hard enough to follow this without being able to hear me.
So anyway, in the opening of this long dialogue with Ananda.
Oh, I didn't finish my thought about Ananda.
He's super brilliant and memorized everything.
Good idea, Bob, maybe.
But there's a way that Ananda just couldn't get it.
He didn't have it in his bones.
In the language of Buddhism, you would say he wasn't an arhat, he wasn't awakened, for a long, long time.
His brother monks are popping off into full awakening constantly, and he's just like, "Ah, I don't get it."
So the Shurangama Sutra opens with Ananda screwing up, and it's actually a little racy.
Ananda is on his daily begging rounds.
The monks would go into town and beg for food every morning.
It's their practice.
They'd go back to their camp and eat their one meal.
Pretty big meal, though, so don't feel too bad for them.
One big meal a day, and then the Buddha would give a talk and they'd practice late into the night.
So Ananda's in town on his begging rounds and he's on his own.
The Chinese commentators to the sutra say that's a mistake already.
You shouldn't be on your own.
You might do something you regret.
Which is part of why we're not on our own.
Have you noticed that?
As a compromise, we let people sleep in their own room.
Even that's a little dodgy.
Somebody should be watching your problem, making sure you don't get into trouble.
It's true.
But anyway, what happens is Ananda goes to one of the houses on his begging rounds and falls in love with the woman who opens the door.
Maybe he knew her before, it doesn't say.
He falls so hard in love that next thing you know they've hopped into bed together.
No kidding, it says that in the sutra.
But luckily for Ananda, his teacher, the Buddha, has clairvoyance.
He always knows what's happening with everyone.
We still had the Buddha here, where he could do better understanding meditation.
Just look into everybody's minds.
See.
In this case, the Buddha was actually in the middle of giving a talk over lunch to an important donor.
Bad timing.
But he cuts it short, and he dispatches the Bodhisattva of wisdom, Manjushri, off to go get Ananda.
Go pick this kid up quick.
It's like getting your teenager.
Don't tell anybody this, but we think our sixteen-year-old teenager might have fallen in love.
Anyway, it's secret and I don't have clairvoyance.
Thank goodness he doesn't listen to my dharma talks.
If he does listen to this ten years from now, he'll probably forgive me.
These things happen.
The interesting thing here is that Manjushri does go get Ananda, and gets there in time, before he breaks his monastic vows.
Actually that would be a big one to break in the ethical system.
You get disrobed and stuff.
Interestingly, the woman he's with, although she is sadly unnamed, returns too.
She comes too, and she hears the teachings too.
Later in the sutra she gets enlightened before Ananda does.
So that's pretty good.
There is also some misogynistic stuff in there that I'm just going to skip.
So it's not great.
It's still patriarchal literature, a thousand years old, but she does get enlightened.
Anyway, the Buddha realized the problem isn't whether Ananda knows enough stuff.
Ananda knows the teachings, he knows how to practice, he knows what the rules are.
He's got it all memorized.
The problem is something about the way Ananda's understanding of reality and himself is off.
That's the basic idea in Buddhism, especially the later Buddhists in China and Japan and Vietnam and other places.
They really emphasize this.
It's not so much the information or the techniques.
It's the understanding.
There's something you're not understanding about who and what you are and how reality really is.
You're a little bit off, a little distorted.
But you're so in the middle of your own distorted reality that you think it's reality, right?
Your belief in reality, which is confirmed by all your thoughts and senses and so on, is pretty stubborn.
And just some teacher, even if they're a glowing Buddha, telling you it's not that way, you're like, "What do you mean?"
So sometimes the Buddha would prescribe meditations, which is kind of what we're doing.
We're doing lots of meditation, right?
We could have three talks a day.
We could have lots of talks.
Maybe that would be better.
We have meditation and one talk a day.
But this sutra is more about using logic and information to gradually talk him out of his confused sense of self and reality.
So it actually uses logic, in a very persistent, grueling way.
I've taken a few stabs at this sutra and I haven't yet finished it, but I'm thinking this might be the time.
I might make it this time.
We'll see.
I just want to give you a little flavor of this.
We don't have time to really do it enough for it to be actually useful, but it's good to get a flavor of the many kinds of Buddhism.
There are many Buddhisms.
This emerged in Chinese literature just a little before the Zen stories, like the story of [unclear: "Yunnan and Dao"].
Not usually, a couple centuries before.
The interesting thing about the Mahayana sutras is that mostly they're pretty long.
Mahayana is the later Buddhist movement, and they tended to have schools around each sutra.
There's one school that loved the Lotus Sutra; that's what they studied.
There's also a school that loved the Shurangama Sutra; that's what they studied.
In each case the students of the sutra, and the sutra itself, will always very thoroughly tell you this is the best one.
And they have good reasons.
This particular translation is by the students of the Chinese master Xuan Hua.
Xuan Hua started a large Buddhist community in California near Ukiah, which hopefully isn't on fire right now, called the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas.
This is the main thing they study there.
He's passed now, but his disciples carry it on.
One of the neat things about the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is that it's one of the few places that really integrates Asian Buddhists and Western convert Buddhists.
There are Chinese monks and American monks all mixed together.
Most places they end up very separate.
Someone was kind enough to point out to me that here we are, apparently in a lineage of Buddhism that came through Japan and China, and look who's talking here. [unclear: "Look out for us"].
Anyway, one of the things Master Hua says in the commentary early on is basically that if you dislike this sutra or don't understand this sutra, that's a very good reason to study it.
Because you don't understand it, that's why you should study it, not the other way around.
Of course you could apply that to just about anything, but I've come to love that kind of devotional logic.
It's really good.
So Ananda gets back in front of the Buddha after this incident, and here's what happens.
I'm quoting the sutra now.
*When Ananda saw the Buddha he bowed and wept in sorrow.
He regretted that since time without beginning he had devoted himself to erudition, but had not fully developed his practice of the path.

Respectfully and repeatedly he asked the Buddha to explain for him the elementary steps that lead to [unclear: "entertainment"] in the wondrous practices of calming the mind, contemplative insight, and meditation on stillness, the practices through which Buddhas from all directions become fully awakened.*
So that's pretty impressive, I think.
After a big mess-up, a big mistake, as a senior practitioner, Ananda is really showing us that the key ingredient here is not your brilliance but your humility.
When you screw up, you don't make excuses or blame anyone.
You didn't blame the woman in this case, right?
You also don't keep it to yourself and try to hide it or navigate around it or come up with a brilliant new strategy so you don't do that again.
Thank goodness nobody noticed, right?
In this case they didn't notice, but you fess up and you ask for teachings.
Which was also instructive to me, back to our practice together in the Dokusan room.
So often people want a strategy.
We want to figure out our problem.
And I like strategies.
I have some good ones, actually.
But maybe it's more helpful if we go back to the basics.
Which makes me think of another of my oft-repeated stories.
But this one I'm going to indulge in especially because it happened right here in this campground, twenty-five years ago, more or less.
We were putting together the first sesshin.
Norman Fischer was coming, which was a big deal, and we were a very young group and not that many of us.
Maybe twenty people were going to be here.
Elizabeth was here.
And I ended up in charge, as I tend to do.
I'm running around like mad trying to figure out what should go where and how to arrange it, all these things that we already have figured out.
None of that was figured out, so everything had to be figured out from scratch, and people actually came and it somehow got started.
This was before you could wear a heart monitor on your wrist.
I don't know what my heart rate was, but pretty high.
I'm not that aware of it, but I'm actually thinking, what's going to go wrong?
I didn't have conscious thoughts of what was going to go wrong, but it's that kind of state.

I went to Dokusan and I'm [unclear: "jammering"] on a million words a minute about how amazing this is, this is all happening, and does he think it's organized right, and there are so many new people here and Norman.
Should we have more introductory materials, and should I offer Zazen instruction, and da da da da da.
I'm going on.
He listens very patiently for a while.
Then he cuts in and says, "You know what's great, Tim?"
I say, "What?"
And he says, "Breathing.
It's really great.
You can feel the breath coming in.
It fills the belly.
You stay with that.
It's so beautiful.
Don't you think it's so beautiful?"
He did it really nicely.
There's not a hint of correction, or "Calm down, son."
It's just breathing.
So anyway, Ananda in the story actually invites that.
I did not have the wherewithal to say, "I'm really freaking out, please give me a basic teaching.
How do you say Zazen?"
But Ananda is able to ask for that, so that's a sign of his maturity in practice, despite what happened in town.
And the Buddha does this.
He says, let me ask you something.
*You and I are members of the same family and we share the affection that is natural among relatives.

Well, at the time you first made the resolve to become enlightened, what excellent attributes did you see in my Dharma that immediately led you to reject the deep familial affection and conjugal love found in the world?*
In other words, what inspired you?
Ananda, think back.
What inspired you to become a monk, to make this huge commitment to devote yourself to practice?
And Ananda says, basically, well, it was seeing you, Buddha.
It was seeing your excellent qualities.
There's a whole thing in traditional Buddhism about how Buddhas exhibit special characteristics, and they talk about that for a long time.
When you become a Buddha, for instance, suddenly all these natural tattoos appear.
On the bottom of your feet there's an image of a Dharma wheel.
Lots of stuff like that.
Things change in the geometry of your body and everybody knows you're a Buddha.
Like the weird little hair things they have.
That's natural when you're a Buddha.
So that's what Ananda says: I saw the marks of awakening in you, and whoa, it changed everything.
And the Buddha sees that there's something really important in this idea Ananda just expressed, that I saw something, I saw something in you.
The Buddha realized this is a teaching opportunity to completely deconstruct, for a thousand pages, the idea of "I see."
What is the I in "I see"?
What does it mean to see?
Who is it that sees?
Do you think it's the eyes that see?
Well, what are eyes?
Where are they located?
How does it all work?
It's all stuff that we do so automatically, right?
We say, "Oh, I see that.
There it is, plain as day, right in front of my face.
That's reality."
Somebody was telling me that they were in just the right position in the room where a couple of the pillars were perfectly lined up.
Actually it's not that hard.
And then she said, "I counted the pillars," and I said, "There's not eight pillars, there's seven pillars."
What are you talking about?
This is seven.
Not eight?
Tim's wrong.
There's seven.
Weird, yeah?
And then, oh, there's eight.
So right when you see seven pillars, you actually see seven pillars, and you know you're right.
So let me just read you a couple of pages of this dialogue.
Hopefully you'll find it entertaining.
Bob, this might go on a little longer than a standard talk, so hopefully you're okay in the kitchen.
This style of teaching takes a little getting used to, but the more styles of teaching we can access, the more tools we have available.
Oh, the other thing is, before Buddha starts questioning Ananda about the nature of seeing, he reaches out.
It says in here, let me read you this.
It's so beautiful.
Where'd it go?
Oh yeah.
*He extended his golden-hued arm and circled his hand on the crown of Ananda's head.
Did this for a minute.*
And we actually retain that gesture in the Zen Dharma transmission ceremony.
Your teacher reaches out and [unclear: "robs"] your head.
So this is like the Buddha was willing to challenge his students, but it's very loving.
Okay, so here's the sutra.
I'll try not to comment, because I don't think it'll take even longer.
We'll do two or three exchanges.
*Now Ananda says the Buddha, I ask you this.
In response to the marks of the Buddha you first made the resolve to attain full awakening.
Just what was it that saw those marks?
And who was it that took delight in them and loved them?
Ananda said to the Buddha, Buddha, I delighted in them and loved them with my mind and my eyes.
Because I saw with my eyes the excellent marks of the Buddha, my mind admired and delighted in them.
In this way I became resolved to extricate myself from death and rebirth and join [unclear: "the Zen"].*
*Buddha said to Ananda, it is as you say, your mind and eyes were the reason for admiration and delight.
Someone who does not know where his mind and eyes are will not be able to overcome the stress of engagement with perceived objects.
Consider for example when bandits invade a country and the king sends forth his soldiers to drive them out.
The soldiers must first know where the bandits are.
Is it the fault of your mind and eyes that you are bound to the cycle of death and rebirth?
I am now asking you something important.
Precisely where are your mind and eyes?*
*World honored one, Ananda said to the Buddha, all beings in all the worlds know that their conscious mind dwells in the body.
And as I regard the beautiful eyes of the Buddha, I know they are part of the Buddha's face.
Clearly they are also part of his body.
And it is evident that these physical organs which respond to perceived objects are part of my face and so part of my conscious mind too.
Surely this is all found in my body.*
Logical, huh?
*The Buddha said to Ananda, when you sit in the Dharma hall of the Buddha, you can see Prince Jeta's grove.
Where is the grove?*
So they are in a building with trees all around.
*We are in the building.
Surely you can see the grove.
Where is the grove?*
*Ananda, this great and sacred Dharma hall with its many stories, world honored one, is in the garden of the benefactor.
It is in Prince Jeta's grove, and Prince Jeta's grove is outside the hall.*
*Ananda, what is the first thing you can see from your place in the hall?*
*Well, Buddha, here in the hall, I am looking first at the Buddha.
I can also see the great assembly, and then as I gaze out, I see the grove in the park.*
